messages.subject: RE: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
parts:
Silvi—

You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.

--Ed Rigdon

 

Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.

Dr. Rigdon,

I very much appreciate your reply and insight. Thank you for sharing the Wu & Estabrook article. If the intercepts are supposed to be constrained on each item, shouldn't the degrees of freedom increase by at least 13 (since there are 13 items)? Thank you!

On Fri, Apr 24, 2020 at 1:32 PM Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

Silvi—

You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.

--Ed Rigdon

 

Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.

Silvi—

     As I meant to imply, lavaan is relaxing other constraints (which are no longer needed for identification) as it imposes the new constraints to achieve scalar invariance. Terrence Jorgensen has (or was working on) some didactic materials to make the fairly deep Wu and Estabrook insights a bit more clear.

     But you might learn a bit by examining the different outputs closely. Parameter estimates are changing from fixed to free while others are changing from free to fixed.

On Fri, Apr 24, 2020 at 1:32 PM Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

Silvi—

You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.

On Fri, Apr 24, 2020 at 1:32 PM Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

Silvi—

You have declared observed variables as ordinal. Recent research (Wu & Estabrook 2016) has made the point that identification of ordinal variable models involves constraints on thresholds as well as loadings and intercepts. Different sets of constraints are required in different situations. So what is happening is that, as you impose more constraints, going from configural to metric to scalar invariance, other constraints are being relaxed. That is why your DF increase less than you expect. There should be lavaan documentation now that offers more specifics on what lavaan does by default.

--Ed Rigdon

 

Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045.

messages.subject: Re: MGCFA Scalar Invariance DF only change by 1. Why?
parts: If the intercepts are supposed to be constrained on each item, shouldn't the degrees of freedom increase by at least 13 (since there are 13 items)? In my case from Metric to Scalar, it decreased by 1. Perhaps this means something is incorrect with my code.....?

The intercepts are already constrained to 0 (and therefore equal) by default.  You only have binary items, so you need to simultaneously constrain c("loadings","thresholds") and compare that model to the default configural model.  If you inspect your output more carefully, you will notice that your df did not increase when you (thought that you) added constraints on intercepts.  The df decreased by 1, indicating you estimated an additional parameter.  This occurred because asking lavaan to constrain intercept for you forced lavaan to assume this was a valid choice (even though they were already constrained), and that meant it proceeded with its default behavior to free the latent mean in the second group (which was your extra parameter).

If you instead constrained thresholds, that would trigger lavaan to free the latent scales (of y*) in group 2, which would no longer need to be fixed to 1 for identification.  Comparing that model to your metric-invariance model would show the same df but different fit (non-nested / nonequivalent models), verifying what I said above: you must compare the model with group.equal = c("loadings","thresholds") to the default configural model.  With binary items, you cannot separately test metric and scalar invariance; only an omnibus test of scalar invariance.  If violated, there is no way to distinguish which parameters are the source of violation (thresholds, intercepts, or loadings).

If you work with ordinal items with more than 2 categories, you could find the semTools::measEq.syntax() function helpful for writing lavaan scripts that write the appropriate constraints for you.  It doesn't bring much benefit for binary items though, since you can make do the comparison I described above.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
